explain.say: Imagine six thousand men on a hillside in Athens, the Pnyx, voting by a show of hands on whether to go to war. That was democracy, from demos, people, and kratos, power. Look at the timeline: it began with Cleisthenes's reforms in 508 BCE and ended in a long war with Sparta.

explain.say: Who actually got a vote? Look at the sizes. A Council of 500 chosen by lot, an Assembly that needed 6,000 for some decisions, and about 40,000 adult male citizens. But Attica, the territory of Athens, had perhaps 300,000 people. Women, foreign residents called metics, and enslaved people had no vote. Was Athens a democracy by our standards?

In 431 BCE war broke out between Athens and Sparta. The historian Thucydides, an Athenian general, wrote that the deepest cause was the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta. Athens had turned the Delian League, an alliance against Persia, into its own empire. Why might fear matter as much as any quarrel?

explain.say: Look at the map. In 415 BCE Athens sent a huge fleet to conquer Syracuse in Sicily. By 413 it was destroyed, and thousands of Athenians died or were enslaved in the quarries. Thucydides tells it as a tragedy of overconfidence. What warning could a modern government take from this?

explain.say: Athens surrendered in 404 BCE. Today the political scientist Graham Allison speaks of a Thucydides trap, when a rising power alarms a ruling one, though many classicists say this oversimplifies Thucydides. Great work. Exam tip: when you cite Thucydides, remember he was a participant with his own view.

faq.q: Who could vote in ancient Athens?
faq.a: Only adult male citizens, probably about 30,000 to 60,000 men at different times. Women, metics, which means resident foreigners, and enslaved people were excluded, though they made up most of the population.

Citizens met in the Assembly to debate and vote directly on laws and war. A Council of 500, chosen by lot each year, prepared business, large citizen juries judged cases, and ostracism could exile a powerful man for ten years.
Thucydides blamed the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta. Immediate quarrels involved Corcyra, Potidaea and Athenian trade sanctions on Megara.
asks: Why did Athens and Sparta fight?

faq.a: A phrase popularised by Graham Allison in 2017 for the danger of war when a rising power threatens a ruling one, based on Thucydides's account. Many historians think it simplifies his much more complex analysis.
Athens's attempt, from 415 to 413 BCE, to conquer Syracuse in Sicily. It ended in total defeat, with the loss of the fleet and thousands of men, and greatly weakened Athens.

facts: Cleisthenes's reforms in Athens date to 508 or 507 BCE.
The Peloponnesian War lasted from 431 to 404 BCE.
Pericles died in 429 BCE during the plague in Athens.

wrong.1: Women, foreigners and enslaved people were excluded.
wrong.2: After Cleisthenes and later reforms, poorer citizens could vote too.

quiz.say: If Attica had about 300,000 people and 40,000 were voting citizens, roughly what share could vote?
quiz.why: 40,000 divided by 300,000 is about 0.13, so roughly 13 percent, on these rough estimates.
